beads.title: Send and understand TSMP rejected-connection messages
beads.description: Upstream has carried TSMP rejected-connection messages (packet.TailscaleRejectedHeader, TSMP type '!') for years, in both directions, and this repository has neither half. SEND: net/tstun/wrap.go's filterPacketInboundFromWireGuard, at commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a, drops an inbound packet on the ACL and then -- when the packet is an IPv4 TCP SYN and TSMP rejects are not disabled -- builds a TailscaleRejectedHeader carrying the reversed four-tuple, the protocol and a reason (RejectedDueToACLs, or RejectedDueToShieldsUp when the filter has shields up), generates it with packet.Generate and injects it outbound to the peer. The comment on it says what it buys: 'Their host networking stack can translate this into ICMP or whatnot as required. But notably, their GUI or tailscale CLI can show them a rejection history with reasons.' Two orderings matter and are part of the port: the peerAPI carve-out just above flips an ACL-refused peerAPI SYN back to Accept before this runs, so a peerAPI SYN never produces a reject; and only IPv4 TCP SYNs produce one, so a non-SYN segment, a UDP datagram or an IPv6 packet dropped by the ACL must stay silent. RECEIVE: wgengine/pendopen.go's trackOpenPreFilterIn parses an inbound reject with Parsed.AsTailscaleRejectedHeader, builds the flow tuple from it, and either marks the pending-open flow as problematic (when the header's MaybeBroken bit is set) or removes the flow and logs 'open-conn-track: flow %v %v > %v rejected due to %v'. It then returns filter.DropSilently for every reason except the app-connector transit-IP one, so the reject is consumed rather than delivered to the local stack. In this repository ts_packet/src/tsmp.rs decodes the disco-key advertisement and nothing else: TSMP_TYPE_REJECTED_CONN is a named constant whose own doc comment says 'Not parsed here'. ts_dataplane::filter_inbound_from_peer consumes the disco advertisement ahead of the ACL and leaves every other TSMP message to inbound_filter_verdict, which accepts it outright ('accepting TSMP inbound (bypasses ACL, Go parity)') and hands it to the smoltcp netstack, which has no handler for IP protocol 99. And nothing on the drop path emits one: inbound_filter_verdict returning false drops the packet with a trace log and no reply. This engine is always the dialing client, which is what makes both halves worth having. Without the receive half, dialling a peer whose ACL refuses us waits out a TCP timeout and the embedder never learns why, where a Go client fails at once with a reason. Without the send half, a Go peer or GUI dialling us into an ACL drop gets the same silence -- and that direction is peer-observable, so it is a divergence a real Tailscale node can see. The work is: marshal and parse TailscaleRejectedHeader against Go's layout in net/packet/tsmp.go (including the flags byte that carries MaybeBroken), emit one from the ACL drop path with the shields-up reason distinguished from the plain ACL one, and consume an inbound one instead of delivering it. Test the refusals, not just the happy path: no reject for a non-SYN, a non-IPv4 or a UDP drop; no reject for a peerAPI-port SYN; a received reject dropped rather than passed to the stack; and a fragmented TSMP still refused before the ACL, as it already is. The connection-rejection aggregator built on top of these events upstream (net/connreject, feature/connreject, nodecap ConnReject and the c2n GET /debug/rejects of capability version 146) is deliberately not part of this: it is diagnostics for a daemon GUI, it sits behind a declared capability version this node holds below, and this bead is closed by the two message halves alone. See PORTING.md section B and section A row 146.

beads.title: Gate the peerAPI DNS proxy on the querying peer, the way Go's replyToDNSQueries does
beads.description: At commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a Go's ipn/ipnlocal/peerapi.go refuses a peerAPI DNS query before resolving anything: handleDNSQuery calls isPeerAPIDNSAllowed and answers '403 DNS access denied' when it returns false. The gate has two arms. A peer that is untagged and owned by the same user (IsSelfUntagged, tightened from a plain isSelf by commit a4c790224 so that a tagged node no longer gets the shortcut) is allowed. Otherwise the default hook requires this node to be OfferingExitNode() or OfferingAppConnector() AND the peer to pass filter.CheckTCP(remoteIP, 0.0.0.0 or 2000:: by family, 53) == Accept, i.e. control's ACL must actually grant that peer internet access through us. The same commit also lets an extension narrow the decision per name (DNSNameFilter), which is the conn25 half and has no counterpart here. Upstream needs the check inside the handler because peerAPI deliberately bypasses the packet filter: net/tstun/wrap.go flips an ACL-refused inbound SYN back to Accept when its destination is the peerAPI port, with the comment 'Let peerapi through the filter; its ACLs are handled at L7, not at the packet level.' This repository has neither half of that design. ts_runtime/src/peerapi.rs's route_conn runs validate_peerapi_request (Go's validatePeerAPIRequest, the anti-DNS-rebinding Host/Origin check) and then hands anything that is not Taildrop or ingress to ts_runtime/src/peerapi_doh.rs, whose server_decide applies exactly two rules: control's ExitNodeFilteredSet (REFUSED) and the fork's forward_exit_egress opt-in, which gates recursion but says nothing about which peer asked. So on a node that has opted into exit egress, any peer whose packets reach the peerAPI port gets recursive resolution through this node's resolvers whether or not control grants it internet access here; and on any node at all, such a peer gets authoritative MagicDNS answers for this node's tailnet names. There is no packet-level carve-out either, so peerAPI here is reachable only by a peer the ACL already lets reach that port -- stricter than Go for Taildrop, looser than Go for DNS, because the common tailnet ACL is permissive about ports and specific about internet access, which is exactly what CheckTCP(..., 53) tests. The work is a source gate in peerapi_doh, evaluated once per connection before any resolution: resolve the connection's source address to a peer (PeerTracker::peer_by_tailnet_ip), ask the live packet filter (ts_runtime::packetfilter) whether that source would be accepted for TCP port 53 to an off-tailnet destination, and answer 403 when it would not. The decision to make is what to do with Go's self arm: this fork has no isSelf notion on the peerAPI path, so the safe reading is to implement the ACL arm only and let a same-user peer be admitted by the ACL like any other -- say which way you went and why. Do not disturb the deliberate divergence recorded in peerapi_doh's module docs, where this server answers some names authoritatively that Go forwards: that divergence is about which names, this bead is about which peers. Test both directions, since a gate that never refuses and a gate that always refuses both look like 'no bug' from one side: a peer the filter accepts for port 53 still gets its answer, and a peer it does not gets 403 and no resolution -- with forward_exit_egress on, so the refusal is the gate's and not the egress opt-in's. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Admit inbound TCP non-SYN and ICMP responses without an ACL rule, as Go's runIn4 does
beads.description: Go's inbound packet filter accepts three classes of packet before consulting any rule, all of them replies to something this node started. In wgengine/filter/filter.go at commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a, runIn4 and runIn6 accept an inbound TCP segment that is not a SYN unconditionally -- the comment explains it: 'For TCP, we want to allow outgoing connections, which means we want to allow return packets on those connections. To make this restriction work, we need to allow non-SYN packets (continuation of an existing session) to arrive. This should be okay since a new incoming session can't be initiated without first sending a SYN.' They accept an ICMP echo response or an ICMP error unconditionally ('ICMP responses are allowed'). And other ICMP matches IPs-only, ignoring ports. This repository ports the third and neither of the first two. ts_dataplane::inbound_filter_verdict (ts_dataplane/src/lib.rs) runs Go's pre() fragment and unknown-protocol drops, accepts TSMP, and then calls filter.can_access with a ts_packetfilter::PacketInfo carrying only { src, dst, ip_proto, port } -- no TCP flags and no ICMP type -- so the non-SYN carve-out is not merely missing, it cannot be expressed in the type the filter matches on. (ts_packetfilter/src/rule.rs does implement Go's matchIPsOnly for ICMP and portless protocols, so the third class is already right; leave it alone.) What this costs depends on the tailnet's ACL, which is why it has gone unnoticed. Under a permissive 'accept everything' policy every reply matches a rule anyway. Under a policy that grants this node outbound access to a peer without granting that peer inbound access back -- an ordinary shape -- the SYN-ACK for this node's own connection arrives at an ephemeral destination port, no rule matches, and the connection hangs. It looks like a network fault, not a filter decision. The same policy silently drops the echo reply to a ping. The work is to carry the TCP flags and the ICMP type into PacketInfo (ts_packet already decodes both), accept a non-SYN TCP segment and an ICMP echo-response or error ahead of the rule match, and keep everything else as it is. The negative case is what gives the change its value and must be asserted: an inbound TCP SYN with no matching rule is still dropped, or the carve-out becomes an open door; likewise an ICMP echo REQUEST with no rule is still subject to the IPs-only match rather than admitted as a 'response'. The stateful half of Go's reply admission -- the UDP/SCTP reverse-flow cache -- is tracked separately because it is a different change with different risk; this bead is closed by the stateless carve-outs alone. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Track outbound UDP flows so their replies are admitted without an explicit ACL rule
beads.description: Go's filter keeps connection-tracking state for UDP and SCTP. In wgengine/filter/filter.go at commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a, Filter.state holds a flowtrack cache bounded at lruMax = 512; RunOut calls UpdateOutboundFlowState, which for UDP and SCTP inserts the REVERSED tuple (proto, dst, src); and runIn4/runIn6 consult that cache first for those protocols and return Accept with the reason 'cached' on a hit, before any rule is matched. Commit e0677ccc7 is the part that names this repository's exact situation: packets produced by netstack -- 'used by tailscaled with --tun userspace-networking, by tsnet, and by the SOCKS5/HTTP proxies' -- enter the wrapper through InjectOutbound and take the injectedRead path, which bypasses RunOut, so the reverse tuple was never recorded and 'a netstack-side dial of UDP would send fine but the reply would be dropped as no matching rule'. Upstream fixed it by exporting UpdateOutboundFlowState and calling it from net/tstun/wrap.go's injected path. Here there is no connection tracking at all to fix. ts_packetfilter's own module docs say so ('this fork's filter is stateless -- it has no TCP-flow tracking'), and ts_packetfilter_state is about ruleset state from a MapResponse, not about flows. ts_dataplane::process_outbound (ts_dataplane/src/lib.rs) runs the capture tee, the host-injected-TSMP drop and the routing, and records nothing; ts_dataplane::inbound_filter_verdict goes straight to the rule match for UDP. And the path upstream had to special-case is not an edge case here, it is the only path this engine has: every outbound packet comes from the netstack. So an embedder that sends a UDP datagram to a peer gets the reply dropped unless control's ACL happens to name the ephemeral source port back -- which it cannot. The work is a small reverse-flow cache: insert (proto, dst, src) for every outbound UDP and SCTP packet in process_outbound, consult it for those protocols at the top of the UDP arm of inbound_filter_verdict, and take the bound from Go (512 entries) rather than inventing one. Assert the refusals as well as the admission, because a cache that admits too much is the failure mode that matters: an inbound UDP datagram with no matching outbound flow and no rule is still dropped; an entry does not admit a datagram from a different source address or port; and the cache is bounded, so a peer cannot grow it without limit. Read this together with the stateless reply carve-outs (TCP non-SYN and ICMP responses), which are the other half of Go's reply admission and are tracked as their own bead because they need no state; this bead is closed by the UDP/SCTP flow cache and its use on both paths. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Rank exit-node suggestions on recent per-region latency, not on one partial netcheck report
beads.description: Upstream used to rank exit-node candidates by their home DERP region's latency in the most recent netcheck report, and changed it because netcheck alternates full reports (every region) with incremental ones (the home region plus a handful of the fastest): 'When the most recent report is incremental, the suggestion fell back to a random for exit nodes that are far away.' At commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a, ipn/ipnlocal/local.go's suggestExitNodeUsingDERP takes preferredRegionID plus a regionLatency map obtained from netcheck.Client.RecentRegionLatency() -- the lowest latency seen per region across the retained report history -- and net/netcheck/netcheck.go ties that history's retention window to the full-report interval (maxAge = fullReportInterval + ReportTimeout) so it is guaranteed to contain one full report, with TestRecentReportsRetainFullNetcheck asserting exactly that. This repository ports the pre-change shape. ts_runtime/src/exit_node_suggest.rs's suggest_exit_node takes a single &NetcheckReport, and min_latency_derp_region -- a faithful port of Go's minLatencyDERPRegion, down to treating a region with no measurement as the maximum duration and tie-breaking on the lower region id -- returns None when the winning region has no measurement at all, at which point the caller falls back to select_region, a uniform random pick. There is no history to fall back on: ts_runtime/src/derp_latency.rs measures and publishes a DerpLatencyMeasurement, keeping nothing. The reason this bites harder here than it did upstream is this fork's own measurement contract. ts_netcheck::Config defaults to complete_threshold: 3 -- the measurement ends as soon as three regions have answered, and in any case at report_timeout (5s) -- so a report against a real DERP map names a handful of regions rather than all of them, every single time, not merely on incremental runs. A candidate exit node homed anywhere else is ranked against nothing, and Device::suggest_exit_node returns a uniformly random region's candidate rather than the nearest one. The work is a per-region best-latency history: keep the lowest latency seen per region over a retention window in the latency measurer or its actor, tie that window to the re-measure cadence the way upstream ties it to fullReportInterval, and change suggest_exit_node to take (preferred_region, region_latency) instead of the report. Keep the injected select_region/select_node closures -- they are a port of Go's selectRegionFunc and selectNodeFunc and they are what makes the algorithm testable. The test worth copying is upstream's: run many measurements, most of them partial, and assert that every region still has a latency to rank on afterwards; then assert the ranking itself, that a candidate in a region measured only several minutes ago still beats an unmeasured one instead of falling to the random pick. See PORTING.md section B.

beads.title: Resolve subdomains of peers that carry the dns-subdomain-resolve node attribute
beads.description: Upstream added a node capability, tailcfg/nodecap's DNSSubdomainResolve ('dns-subdomain-resolve'), which when control sets it on a node means that all of that host's subdomains resolve to the same addresses. At commit 3945b82f8a9550b54c33e61d4ed2227862d53e8a, net/dns/resolver/tsdns.go carries a SubdomainHosts set of FQDNs beside its Hosts map, documented as 'a set of FQDNs from Hosts that should also resolve subdomain queries to the same IPs', and on a lookup miss the resolver walks the queried name's parents (util/dnsname's Parent) looking for one that is a subdomain host, either in that set or via the MagicDNS host index's SubdomainHost predicate. A subdomain may have several labels: for a node named machine, both my.machine and be.my.machine match. Because it is driven by a node attribute that control sets per node, upstream needed no capability version for it -- a node without the attribute is unaffected. Nothing in this repository implements it. The string dns-subdomain-resolve appears nowhere in the tree, and ts_runtime/src/magic_dns.rs resolves peer names by exact match against the DNS view's name index, so a subdomain of a peer name is NXDOMAIN here whatever control says. A tailnet that has turned the attribute on gets working subdomain resolution from every Go client and NXDOMAIN from this one, which is a difference an embedder cannot diagnose from this side. The work is to plumb the attribute onto the DNS view (the node capability is already carried on ts_control::Node's cap_map, and DnsView is built from the peer set) and add the parent walk to the peer-name lookup in magic_dns. The cases to pin are the ones that keep the walk from becoming a wildcard: a node WITHOUT the attribute must still answer NXDOMAIN for its subdomains; an exact name must still beat a parent match; the walk must stop at the tailnet zone rather than climbing past it into names this node is not authoritative for; and the multi-label case (be.my.machine) must resolve, since one level of parent is not what upstream implements. The peerAPI DoH server shares magic_dns's decide, so check that the behaviour reaching that path is the one you intend. See PORTING.md section B.
